edition: Newton, Principia, Andrew Motte trans., 1729 (Wikisource); Book I, Section II, Proposition VII; Plate 3, Figure 3.

figures.caption: If a body revolves in the circumference of a circle, find the law of centripetal force directed to any given point.

text.latex: Proposition VII is the first concrete application of the force-measure proved in \textcolor{radgreen}{Proposition VI},      now applied to the simplest curvilinear orbit: the \textcolor{circblue}{circle $VQPA$}.      A body $P$ revolves in the circumference and $Q$ is the next place into which it moves.      The remarkable freedom here is that the \textcolor{centerorange}{force centre $S$} need not sit at the centre $O$ —      it may lie anywhere inside the circle, and we still seek the law along the \textcolor{radgreen}{radius $SP$},      which is the distance whose powers Prop. VI taught us to track.

At the body's place we draw the \textcolor{tanteal}{tangent $PRZ$}, the forceless straight path the body would keep      without any centripetal pull — this is the heart of the deviation argument.      Through the force centre we draw the \textcolor{diampurple}{chord $PV$}, and through $V$ the \textcolor{diampurple}{diameter $VA$}, joining $AP$.      Because $VA$ is a diameter, the angle $VPA$ inscribed in the semicircle is a right angle,      and this single fact seeds the chain of similar triangles that will follow.      The \textcolor{diampurple}{chord $PV$ through $S$} is the intrinsic length that will ultimately govern the whole force law.

Now we lay down Prop. VI's apparatus: \textcolor{constred}{$QT$ perpendicular to $SP$} and \textcolor{constred}{$LR$ parallel to $SP$},      meeting the tangent at $R$ and $Z$ and the circle at $L$.      The similar triangles $ZQR$, $ZTP$, $ZPA$ give $RP^2$ (that is $QR\cdot L$) to $QT^2$ as $AV^2$ to $PV^2$,      so multiplying by $SP^2/QR$ and letting $Q$ coincide with $P$ collapses the \textcolor{constred}{construction} into the clean chord-cube.      Substituting into Prop. VI yields $F \propto \dfrac{1}{SP^2\cdot PV^3}$; and in the special case where $S$ sits at $O$,      the chord $PV$ becomes the diameter and the law reduces to the pure inverse-square $1/SP^2$. \textit{Q.E.D.}

ceiling_equations.latex: QR\cdot L : QT^2 = AV^2 : PV^2 \;\Rightarrow\; F \propto \dfrac{1}{SP^2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{PV^3}
